div.head: This paper considers the problem of preemptive hard real-time scheduling of sporadic graph tasks on a uniprocessor with Earliest Deadline First (EDF).
div.p: A sporadic graph task associated to an application is characterized by a set of subtasks under precedence constraints with deadline constraints. We study feasibility conditions based on the computation of the worst case response time of any subtask of a graph task. We investigate the late deadline constraint.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: We consider in this paper the problem of hard real-time scheduling of sporadic graph tasks with Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling. A graph task is composed of a set of subtasks with precedence constraints. We establish feasibility conditions to ensure that every subtask of a graph respects timeliness properties. The timeliness properties investigated in this paper are late deadlines imposed on the response time of every subtask. The worstcase response time of any subtask in a graph task depends on the precedence constraints of the subtasks and the scheduling chosen to schedule the subtasks with no precedence constraints. Real-time scheduling has been extensively studied in the last thirty years. Feasibility conditions for independent preemptive sporadic task scheduled using EDF was introduced by [2], [1], [9]. [8], [6] showed how to compute the worst case response time of a simple sporadic task. This result was extended to the non-preemptive case by [6], [4] and [9]. In 1973, [12] presented an optimal algorithm that minimizes the maximum lateness of a set of tasks with precedence relations and simultaneous arrival times. [13], [14] solved the problem of scheduling tasks with precedence constraints by changing their relative deadlines. The feasibility analysis for graph tasks with preemptive scheduling for fixed priority scheduling was proposed by [7]. The solution is based on a graph transformation into a chain. The chain is used to establish the response time of a graph task. This approach was further developed by [10] in the case of re-entrant graph for mixed preemptive and non preemptive subtasks with fixed priority scheduling.

We use the same approach as in [7] but consider non reentrant graph tasks. We show how to transform a graph task into a chain and study the worst case response time of a subtask in its chain. The scheduling of independent subtasks is EDF. We first define the concepts and notations in section 2. We describe the sporadic graph model and show how to transform a graph into a chain. In section 3, we propose a feasibility condition for preemptive EDF graph task scheduling. We illustrate the feasibility conditions by an example in section 4. Finally, we conclude.

div.head: Notations
div.p: In this paper, we consider a set τ = {τ 1 ,…,τ n } of n sporadic graph tasks. A Sporadic graph task τ i , is defined by: • G i : a graph of subtasks with precedence constraints,

• T i : the minimum inter-arrival time, abusively called the period of the graph task By definition, G i (τ i )={τ i 1 ,…τ i ni } is the set of n i preemptive subtasks composing the graph G i . Notice that a subtask can be pre-empted. A partial order is defined for the subtasks, the order specifying operation precedence constraints. τ i j < τ i k , means that τ i j must be completed before τ i k . In this paper, we consider the non-re-entrant graph tasks. A graph task is called non-re-entrant if the (k+1) st instance of the graph task will not be executed until the k th instance of the graph task has been completed A subtask τ i j of a graph task τ i is defined by: • C i j : its execution duration • T i : the minimum inter-arrival time or period (every subtask inherits the period of its graph task). • D i j : the relative deadline of subtask τ i j . We consider the following scheduling:

• Subtasks with precedence constraints are scheduled according to their precedence constraints, whatever their deadlines. • Subtasks with no precedence constraints are scheduled according to preemptive Earliest Deadline First (EDF). EDF schedules the subtasks according to their absolute deadlines: the subtask with the shortest absolute deadline has the highest priority. Ties are broken arbitrarily. • A task τ i , requested at time t 0 results in the activation of all its subtasks. Hence, for any subtask τ i j of G i , its absolute deadline is t 0 + D i j . Property 1: τ i p has a higher priority than τ j q if • τ i p has a smaller absolute deadline than τ j q if either ij or τ i p and τ j q have no precedence constraint • τ i p <τ j q if i=j. Furthermore, we assume that:

• Time is discrete (task arrivals occur and task executions begin and terminate at clock ticks; the parameters used are expressed as multiples of the clock tick); in [11], it is shown that there is no loss of generality with respect to feasibility results through restricting the schedules to being discrete, once the task parameters are assumed to be integers (multiples of the clock tick) i.e. a discrete schedule exists, if and only if a continuous schedule exists. • An idle time t is defined on a processor as a time, such that there are no subtasks released before time t pending at time t. An interval of successive idle times is called an idle period. • A busy period is defined as a time interval [a,b), such that there is no idle time in [a,b) (the processor is fully busy) and such that both a and b are idle times. • Given a non-concrete task set (A task is said to be non-concrete if its request time is not known a priori.), the synchronous busy period is defined as the time interval [0,L) delimited by two successive idle times in the scenario where all tasks are released at the same time [15]. The value of L does not depend on the scheduling algorithm, as far as it is non-idling, but only on the task arrival pattern. L is called the length of the synchronous busy period. The value of L is given is section 3.1.

div.head: Graph to Chain Transformation
div.p: We first show in this section how to transform a graph into a chain of subtasks. This chain of subtasks will be further considered in the real-time analysis of section 5.
The following procedure 1 describes how to transform a graph G i of a task τ i into a chain:
1. Set chain to empty.

div.head: Consider all the subtasks in the graph having no predecessor. Select among these subtasks the subtask, which has the minimum relative deadline, insert it at the end of the current chain and remove it from the graph 3. Proceed to point 2 until the graph is empty Procedure 1: Graph to chain transformation
div.p: After the transformation, the subtasks are indexed by increasing index from τ i 1 , the first subtask to execute, to τ i ni . In the following sections, τ i j therefore represents the j th subtask in the chain obtained from graph G i .

The following lemma proves that this transformation does not change the schedulability problem. Lemma 1: Scheduling the subtasks according to their chain does not change the scheduling order obtained for the subtasks when scheduled according to their graph. Proof: Let ϒ* be the processing order of subtasks of graph G i and ϒ be the scheduling order obtained from the chain of G i . Consider two successive subtasks τ i j and τ i k in ϒ*. We have two cases: (i) the subtasks have precedence constraints (ii) the subtasks have no precedence constraints. In the first case, as the chain is built from the precedence constraints, and from property 1, the execution order of τ i j and τ i k is the same in ϒ. In the second case, from property 1, EDF scheduling is used to arbitrate between τ i j and τ i k . As all the subtasks of a graph are released at the same time (see section 2.1), the absolute deadline used by EDF for subtasks in a graph and subtasks in a chain are the same. Leading to the same processing order equal to ϒ, from procedure 1.

Ƒ We now transform the chain into its canonical form w.r.t a subtask τ i j . This transformation is required for the response time computation of τ i j . This modification consists in changing the relative deadline of a subtask τ i m-1 to the relative deadline of τ i m if its relative deadline is smaller than τ i m , starting from m=j down to m=2. This allows us to obtain a set of consecutive subtasks with equal or decreasing relative deadlines from τ I 1 to τ i j . The relative deadlines of the subtasks after τ i j are left unchanged. The following lemma proves that the completion time of the subtask τ i j in the chain of G i and the completion time of τ i j* in its canonical chain are the same. Lemma 2: The completion time of any subtask τ i j in G i is unchanged considering the same subtasks in its associated canonical chain. Proof: Consider two consecutive subtasks τ i j-1 and τ i j in the chain of G i . We have two cases: (i) D i j-1 > D i j and (ii) D i j-1 D i j . In the first case, by construction the canonical chain will preserve the relative deadlines of the subtasks τ i j-1 and τ i j ҏ . In the second case with the canonical transformation, we obtain D i j-1* =D i j and D i j unchanged. The subtasks scheduled between the absolute deadline of τ i j-1 and τ i j will be scheduled before τ i j-1 but not after τ i j thus leaving unchanged the starting time of τ i j . As subtasks followingҏ τ i j are unchanged, the completion time of τ i j is also unchanged. We give an example of transformation of a graph task into its chain and its canonical form. div.head: Real-Time Analysis
div.p: In this section, we first describe the feasibility conditions of a set of graph tasks. The feasibility analysis is based on the determination of worst-case response time of subtasks of a graph. For that purpose, we first describe the general principles required to determine this worst case response time. We then describe the computation of the worst-case response time of the subtasks in the preemptive case.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we have studied the problem of scheduling graph tasks with EDF preemptive scheduling. We have proposed a sufficient feasibility condition to guarantee that any subtask of a graph meets its deadline. The feasibility condition is based on the computation of worst case response time of a subtask of a graph. We have proposed an example that illustrates the feasibility conditions.
